title: Alexander Zverev to face lawsuit over alleged false statements regarding outcome of domestic abuse case
content:
Alexander Zverev is set to face a new lawsuit over an alleged “false factual assertion” regarding the conclusion of a domestic abuse case against him.

Brenda Patea, Zverev’s former partner and the mother of his daughter, filed a civil lawsuit at Berlin Regional Court II on September 18, seeking an injunction and financial compensation over comments Zverev made to French newspaper “L’Équipe”, in which Zverev said Patea’s allegations of domestic abuse had “been proven false” and that his “innocence had been proven.”

The lawsuit, which was first reported by Bounces, centers on Zverev’s description of a 2024 criminal case that he and Patea settled out of court. Legal proceedings were discontinued without a verdict determining guilt or innocence, and Zverev paid a monetary charge of over $218,000 split between legal costs and charity organizations. The terms of the settlement with Patea have not been disclosed.

Patea alleges the remarks breached an agreement restricting public statements about their previous legal proceedings, because, her lawsuit argues, it is not the case that Zverev was proven innocent. Patea’s lawyers argue his assertion that the allegations were proven false was a factual claim rather than an expression of opinion.

“There is no court order establishing the defendant’s innocence, no final acquittal, or any other decision with corresponding content,” according to the lawsuit.

“This is nothing more than an expression of opinion, protected by the freedom of speech,” Dr. Anna Sophie Heuchemer, a lawyer representing Zverev, told The Athletic by email, describing Zverev’s comments as “a permissible assessment of legal proceedings that have already reached a final, binding conclusion”.

Heuchemer said that neither Zverev nor his legal representatives had been formally served with the lawsuit as of November 13, but confirmed they would defend it once served. Patea’s lawyer, Dr. Michael Scheele, said in an interview that the court had initiated the process of serving Zverev with the lawsuit at his residence in Monaco.

A November 5 court order, obtained by The Athletic, sets out a written preliminary procedure, giving Zverev one month from formal service to indicate whether he intends to defend the claim. The lawsuit was filed after three letters to Zverev went unreturned.

Patea was the second former girlfriend to accuse Zverev of domestic abuse. Olya Sharypova made allegations against him in 2020. She did not pursue charges; a 15-month ATP Tour investigation found there was “insufficient evidence” to substantiate Sharypova’s allegations and Zverev did not face disciplinary action. Zverev called the allegations “unfounded and untrue.”

Following his maiden Grand Slam win at this year’s French Open, Zverev said during an interview with French newspaper L’Équipe, “you know that the accusations have been proven false?”

He was responding to a question about Patea’s claim and later in the interview, Zverev said: “I did everything I could, and my innocence has been proven.”

Patea alleged that Zverev pushed her against a wall and choked her during an argument in 2020, which Zverev has always denied.

She reported the incident to police in October 2021. Two years later, a criminal court in Berlin issued a penalty order of nearly $500,000 against Zverev. Prosecutors can seek such orders if they believe that the evidence in a case is compelling enough that no trial is required.

Zverev contested the order, and called it “complete bull––––” during a news conference at the 2023 Paris Masters.

In May and June of 2024, Berlin’s Tiergarten District Court conducted a trial. On May 31, Zverev’s lawyer at the time, Dr Alfred Dierlamm, requested that Patea’s testimony be heard behind closed doors, which the judge granted.

On June 7, the court announced that, with the consent of the prosecutor’s office, the case had been settled out of court. That terminated the original penalty order. Zverev paid $218,000, not to Patea, but to the state treasury and non-profit organizations.

“The decision is not a verdict and it is not a decision about guilt or innocence. One decisive factor for the court decision was that the witness has expressed her wish to end the trial. The defendant agreed to the termination of the case,” Tiergarten District Court spokesperson Inga Wahlen told The Athletic.

The trial took place during the French Open, where Zverev reached the final, losing to Carlos Alcaraz. In a news conference, he said of the absence of a verdict:

“That’s what dropping the case is. That is innocence. They’re not going to drop the case if you’re guilty at the end of the day. … I don’t know what translations you have, but that’s what it means.”

2026 has been Zverev’s most successful year on court. He has won his first two Grand Slam titles, at the French and U.S. Opens reaching world No. 1 in the process — in part thanks to the prolonged absences of Italy’s Jannik Sinner and Spain’s Alcaraz due to injury. The allegations against him were discussed on ESPN during the U.S. Open final by commentator Mary Carillo.

As he prepared to give a runner-up speech at the 2025 Australian Open, a woman in the crowd shouted out in apparent reference to the allegations: “Australia believes Olya and Brenda! Australia believes Olya and Brenda!”

“I believe there are no more accusations,” Zverev said in his news conference when asked about the incident. “There haven’t been for, what, nine months now. Good for her, I think she was the only one in the stadium who believed anything in that moment.”

He is currently playing the ATP Finals in Turin, Italy, as the No. 1 seed.
